Please read this carefully:

<document>
# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
I've read this one carefully too. It is a much stronger paper than the Halden pilot. It fixes most of what I criticised there:
- It has a randomised control group, so it doesn't rely on self-comparison.
- Output comes from administrative records rather than manager ratings.
- Actual hours come from timesheets rather than the schedule.
- It explicitly tests whether results hold across types of work.

Its results also match that critique. The headline case-processing gain of +12.5% per actual hour is about half Halden's +23.4%. The scheduled-hours figure overstates it by roughly 10 points. Coverage-bound work loses output. The issues below are refinements, not fatal flaws, and a few are genuine inconsistencies worth fixing before publication.

## Arithmetic check

Most figures hold together:
- Actual hours: 37.9 → 33.0 is −12.9%, and 37.6 → 31.2 is −17.0%.
- Output per actual hour: 0.979 / 0.87 gives +12.5%, and 0.886 / 0.83 gives +6.7%.
- The scheduled-hours comparison: 0.979 / 0.8 gives +22.4%.

One small anomaly: in the counter stratum, dividing the output-per-FTE interval by the hours ratio gives about +0.1% to +13.4%. The reported +0.4% to +13.3% is slightly *narrower*, even though uncertainty in hours should widen it. This is plausible if output per hour was estimated directly rather than derived. Since the lower bound is close to zero, state how it was computed.

## Major issues

**1. Ten clusters are too few for standard clustered errors.** The counter stratum has 5 offices per arm. Cluster-robust standard errors are biased downward with so few clusters, so the confidence intervals are probably too narrow. The near-zero lower bound for counter output per hour is the estimate most at risk. Report wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation-inference p-values. With stratified randomisation at office level, randomisation inference is natural.

**2. The registered primary analysis isn't clearly reported.** The registered primary outcome is output per FTE, but the paper reports only results by stratum. Say whether:
- the registered primary analysis was pooled or by stratum;
- the split by type of work was registered as a primary contrast, a secondary analysis, or a test of heterogeneity.

If pooled was primary, report the pooled estimate first. Given the paper's emphasis on registration, readers will look for this.

**3. "Output per FTE" needs a definition under treatment.** If FTE is defined by hours, a 30-hour employee is 0.8 FTE, and output "per FTE" means something very different. Since the definition is not given, it appears to mean output per head at full pay. Define it explicitly.

**4. The counter results suggest demand moved between offices.** Two things point to this:
- *The size of the fall.* If public demand were unchanged, contacts handled would fall roughly in line with the abandonment rate. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10%, which means about 4% fewer calls answered, yet contacts per employee fell 11.4%. Something else is going on. One plausible explanation is that people facing longer waits went to a nearby *control* counter or another channel. That would push treated output down and control output up, and overstate the effect. This breaks the assumption that offices don't affect each other's outcomes, and office-level randomisation does not prevent it.
- *Repeat contacts.* Repeat contacts rose (11.8% against 10.9%), and these count as output, so they hide part of the decline.

Report total incoming demand (calls offered, walk-ins) by arm, and check for diversion of demand where treated and control offices are geographically close.

**5. Part of the counter per-hour gain is probably the queue, not productivity.** With fewer staff present and longer queues, each staff member spends less time idle. Contacts per hour therefore rise because utilisation rose. This happens even if nobody works faster or rests better. The cost appears as public waiting time. The Discussion's line that "each hour worked was somewhat more productive" should acknowledge this. Without it, the +6.7% suggests a benefit that was actually paid for by the public.

**6. Waiting times, abandonment and quality aren't analysed like the primary outcome.**
- Average wait (4.2 → 6.9) and abandonment (6% → 10%) are before-and-after figures for treated offices only, not difference-in-differences against control.
- The quality row ("3.1% v 3.0%", "11.8% v 10.9%") compares levels with no confidence intervals and no pre-period.

These are registered secondary outcomes, so give them the same analysis as the primary. The Results section also never mentions that repeat contacts went up in counter offices.

**7. The appeal overturn rate lags.** Appeals take time to be lodged and decided. Decisions made in months 6–9 mostly won't have resolved appeals by month 9, so "unchanged quality" in case-processing is premature. Report overturn rates by the month the decision was made, and revisit at 24 months.

**8. Backlogs can be measured now.** The Limitations section treats backlog build-up as unknown, but the case-management system already holds it. Report for each arm:
- backlog size;
- the age distribution of open cases;
- the share closed near the statutory deadline.

Keeping cases closed constant by working on a growing queue, or by prioritising easy cases, would look the same as genuine maintenance in the current output measure.

**9. Recorded hours may understate work actually done.** Timesheets capture *claimed* overtime. In case-processing, unclaimed work at home or in breaks is plausible and would inflate the per-hour gain. A short time-use survey or system login data would bound this. Paid overtime, at about 3 hours per week above schedule, also affects cost. The county's real question includes cost per case, and the paper doesn't report it. A simple cost analysis would cover full pay, overtime, and the staffing needed to restore counter waiting times.

## The exploratory meetings analysis

It is caveated well, but it has a flaw and an implication worth drawing out.

- **There is no baseline.** Meeting data were collected only in month six, so "offices that cut meetings most" cannot be computed. The available data support only "offices with fewer meetings at month six". The difference between arms (3.8 against 7.1 hours) could partly reflect where they started. Correct the wording.
- **r = 0.71 across 7 offices** gives p ≈ 0.07. Saying so explicitly helps more than the general caveat.
- **Meetings could explain almost the whole gain.** If treated offices also started at about 7.1 meeting hours, the hours not spent in meetings fall from about 30.8 to 29.2, or −5%. That fits closely with output per FTE of −2.1%. Under that assumption, the gain per non-meeting hour would be only about +3%, so most of the 12.5% would come from cutting meetings rather than from rest. This is speculative because the baseline is missing. Still, it is a sharper statement of the paper's own point, and it gives the confirmatory test at 24 months a concrete target.

## Smaller points

- **Absence of evidence.** "Statistically indistinguishable from control" for case-processing output still allows a loss of up to 6.8%. "Little or no measurable loss" is defensible. A stated equivalence margin would be better.
- **Sick days.** If 30 hours was delivered as fewer days rather than shorter days, there are fewer scheduled days on which to be absent, and part of the −29% is mechanical. State how the rotas were structured, and report absence per scheduled day.
- **Resignations.** 3.9% against 7.4% needs a confidence interval or a count. With about 590 staff per arm over nine months, the numbers are small.
- **Control-group reactions.** The Limitations section notes that staff knew their assignment. If HR or survey data allow, check whether control offices' sick days or resignations moved during the trial. Resentment or demoralisation in the control group would flatter the comparison.

## Summary

This is a careful, honestly reported trial, and its central conclusion is well supported: per-hour and per-employee productivity diverge, most sharply in work tied to presence, and scheduled-hours estimates overstate gains. The most important fixes are to:
1. use inference that is valid with few clusters;
2. clarify the registered primary analysis;
3. investigate demand diversion in the counter stratum;
4. put the service outcomes on the same footing as output;
5. correct the "cut meetings" wording.

If useful, I can draft a referee report covering both papers, or a short note setting the Halden and Varden estimates side by side.
